layers.name: Client Apps
layers.description: Applications create prompts, select a model, and consume streamed tokens through an OpenAI-compatible API. The client owns retries, cancellation, and the user experience.
layers.experiment: The benchmark clients generated controlled chat and RAG traffic.
layers.question: Why stream tokens instead of waiting for the whole answer?
layers.answer: Streaming lowers perceived latency because the user sees the first token while decode continues.

layers.name: Edge
layers.description: DNS, anycast, TLS termination, and DDoS protection bring a request to a healthy region. This layer should reject bad traffic before it reaches expensive inference workers.
layers.experiment: The experiment used direct AWS endpoints and did not implement a production edge.
layers.question: What belongs at the edge rather than the model gateway?
layers.answer: Network termination, DDoS controls, and coarse routing belong at the edge; model-aware policy belongs closer to the gateway.

layers.name: API Gateway
layers.description: The gateway authenticates clients, validates requests, applies quotas, and exposes a stable API even when backends change. It can also meter tokens for billing.
layers.experiment: LiteLLM exposed one API and model names for the two backends.
layers.question: Why not expose every vLLM server directly?
layers.answer: A gateway centralizes policy and keeps backend topology out of client code.

layers.name: Safety
layers.description: Input and output classifiers enforce content and product policy independently of the main model. Separate capacity prevents safety checks from starving generation.
layers.experiment: The experiment did not add a safety classifier.
layers.question: Why run safety on a separate pool?
layers.answer: It isolates policy capacity and lets a small classifier scale independently from expensive generation workers.

layers.name: Router & Scheduler
layers.description: The router selects a backend; the scheduler forms continuous batches on each worker. Good routing considers priority, queue depth, model placement, and prefix-cache affinity.
layers.experiment: LiteLLM routed qwen-fast to the GPU and qwen-batch to the CPU; router overhead was measured.
layers.question: Why route by workload instead of round robin?
layers.answer: Chat and long prompts have different SLOs and resource profiles; round robin can mix conflicting work on the same accelerator.

layers.name: Packaging
layers.description: A deployable image combines the model server, engine, and pinned dependencies. Reproducible packaging prevents runtime drift between nodes.
layers.experiment: The GPU used a Python environment; the CPU used the vLLM CPU container.
layers.question: What should be pinned in an inference image?
layers.answer: Engine, framework, runtime libraries, model revision, and launch configuration should all be versioned.

layers.name: Serving Topology
layers.description: Aggregated serving keeps prefill and decode together. Disaggregation or heterogeneous pools separate work so each pool can scale for its own bottleneck.
layers.experiment: The final test used heterogeneous GPU and CPU pools to isolate chat from RAG.
layers.question: When is disaggregation worth the complexity?
layers.answer: When prefill and decode scale differently enough that independent pools outweigh KV-transfer and operational costs.

layers.name: Inference Engine
layers.description: The engine tokenizes, schedules batches, manages KV pages, runs model steps, samples tokens, and streams output. Engine and model compatibility comes before theoretical performance.
layers.experiment: vLLM 0.29.0 ran on both nodes and was compared with Hugging Face generate.
layers.question: Why did vLLM beat plain generate here?
layers.answer: Continuous batching, lower execution overhead, CUDA graphs, and fused serving kernels improved delivered throughput.

layers.name: KV Cache
layers.description: Attention keys and values are retained for every active sequence. Paging reduces fragmentation; distributed systems can tier or transfer blocks between workers.
layers.experiment: The L4 exposed 575,440 KV tokens; halving the pool did not affect short-chat capacity.
layers.question: Why can a model fit while requests still run out of memory?
layers.answer: Weights may fit, but live sequences consume additional KV cache that grows with context and concurrency.

layers.name: Model Execution
layers.description: The framework executes transformer operations and coordinates tensor, pipeline, data, or expert parallelism when a model spans devices.
layers.experiment: The experiment used one device per node, so distributed model parallelism was not needed.
layers.question: When do you need tensor parallelism?
layers.answer: When one model replica cannot fit or meet latency on a single accelerator, accepting communication overhead across devices.

layers.name: Compiler & Kernels
layers.description: Compilers lower model graphs to device operations. Fused attention and matrix kernels keep data on chip and convert peak specifications into useful tokens per second.
layers.experiment: CUDA kernels served the L4; AMX-optimized CPU kernels served Sapphire Rapids.
layers.question: Why do equal FLOP ratings produce different inference speed?
layers.answer: Kernel coverage, memory traffic, precision support, launch overhead, and workload shape determine achieved performance.

layers.name: Runtime & Drivers
layers.description: The runtime owns device memory, launches kernels, and coordinates collectives. Versions must stay compatible with the engine and host driver.
layers.experiment: The L4 used CUDA 13.2; the CPU path used the vLLM CPU runtime.
layers.question: Why pin driver and runtime versions per pool?
layers.answer: Compatibility mismatches can prevent startup or disable optimized kernels even when application code is unchanged.

layers.name: Accelerators
layers.description: Matrix units supply prefill compute while high-bandwidth memory feeds decode. Memory capacity limits model and KV fit; bandwidth often limits decode.
layers.experiment: Interactive chat ran on an NVIDIA L4; background RAG ran on Intel Xeon with AMX.
layers.question: Why can a GPU cost more per hour but less per token?
layers.answer: Higher throughput can spread hourly cost across far more tokens, provided the workload keeps the GPU utilized.

layers.name: Node
layers.description: A node combines accelerators, host CPUs, DRAM, local storage, and network interfaces. Host CPU capacity still matters for tokenization, routing, and request handling.
layers.experiment: The nodes were g6.xlarge and c7i.4xlarge; the four-vCPU GPU host also ran extra experiment processes.
layers.question: Can a GPU server be bottlenecked by its host CPU?
layers.answer: Yes. Tokenization, APIs, routers, clients, and networking can contend for host cores before the GPU is full.

layers.name: Network Fabric
layers.description: Scale-up links connect devices inside a node; scale-out links carry collectives and KV state between nodes. Frontend traffic should stay separate from model fabric where scale demands it.
layers.experiment: Both nodes communicated over a private VPC network.
layers.question: Why does prefill/decode disaggregation need a fast network?
layers.answer: The prefill worker must transfer KV state to decode workers; slow transfer can erase the benefit of separate pools.

layers.name: Storage
layers.description: Object storage holds model artifacts; local NVMe or peer transfer avoids downloading large checkpoints on every restart. Access controls protect model weights.
layers.experiment: Each node downloaded the model locally; production weight distribution was not tested.
layers.question: Why cache weights near compute?
layers.answer: Faster startup improves recovery and scale-out, while repeated object-store downloads can dominate readiness time.

layers.name: Cluster Management
layers.description: The cluster places workers, exposes services, drains unhealthy nodes, rolls versions, and scales pools. Device operators surface accelerator health to the scheduler.
layers.experiment: Instances were operated manually; autoscaling and multi-AZ recovery were not tested.
layers.question: What should trigger inference autoscaling?
layers.answer: Queue depth, TTFT, running requests, and cache pressure are more useful than GPU utilization alone.

layers.name: Facility
layers.description: Cooling, rack power, UPS, and generators bound how much accelerator capacity a site can host. Dense systems turn thermal design into a software capacity constraint.
layers.experiment: AWS operated the facility; the experiment did not measure it.
layers.question: Why should an inference architect care about cooling?
layers.answer: Power and thermal envelopes cap deployable accelerator density and therefore regional capacity and cost.

layers.name: Power Grid
layers.description: Grid capacity and energy mix set the fleet ceiling, influence regional availability, and affect carbon and long-term operating cost.
layers.experiment: The experiment consumed AWS capacity but did not measure grid effects.
layers.question: How can grid capacity affect an API product?
layers.answer: If a region cannot add powered racks, the service cannot scale there regardless of accelerator supply.
